title: Meristems, Buds, and Apical Dominance
objective: Explain how shoot meristems produce new organs and why removing or bending an apex changes branching.

terms.definition: A region of actively dividing, relatively undifferentiated plant cells.
The growing point that produces the main shoot’s leaves, nodes, and stem tissues.
A meristem at a leaf axil that can develop into a branch or flower-bearing shoot.
Suppression of axillary growth associated with the actively growing shoot apex and hormonal/transport relationships.

coreScience: The shoot apical meristem generates new stem and leaf primordia. Axillary meristems are positioned at nodes and can remain small, grow into branches, or transition toward reproductive development. Plant architecture emerges from which meristems grow, how fast they grow, and how long their internodes become.

Apical dominance is often summarized as “auxin from the top suppresses lower branches,” but the real system involves auxin transport, cytokinins, strigolactones, sugar availability, light, vascular connections, and sink competition. Removing the main apex changes those relationships and commonly releases one or more axillary buds. Bending can reduce the apex’s positional dominance and improve light exposure without removing tissue.

The response is not instant or identical across plants. Stage, genotype, root health, temperature, light, water status, and cut location affect recovery. A cut can also create a wound and remove photosynthetic or future reproductive tissue.
cultivationRelevance: Project procedure THC-GROW-110 requires assessing plant vigor, water status, bud viability, target node, and support before training. This is a risk-control procedure, not a universal biological law. Record the exact node and technique so recovery can be compared.
Judge success by resumed growth, balanced branch development, and absence of wound decline—not simply by the number of new tips.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Bend, top, prune, trellis, or no treatment.
Node, branch order, and remaining growth points.
Stage, water status, vigor, and recent stress.
Days to visible axillary growth and resumed extension.
Shoot count, symmetry, wound condition, and canopy change.

misconceptions: Topping changes genetics: It changes architecture and resource distribution, not the inherited sequence.
More tops always increase yield: More sinks can exceed available light, leaf area, root support, or space.
Auxin alone explains every branch response: Branching is controlled by an interacting network.
evidenceLimits: Training responses are strongly context-dependent. Claims of guaranteed yield or potency increases require controlled evidence.
